As a user, I want to have natural back-and and forth conversations with the Personal Assistant, without the need to explicitly invoke the assistant again via wake-up-word or push-to-talk. 
- ""Extended dialog"" is the official term for customers, internally many folks refer to this behavior as ""Snoozing"", in Alexa it is called ""Follow-up mode""
- Implementation is basically a synthetic speech state
- entered after the assistant goes from speaking to idle (after final Prompt by assistant, Confirmation Sound or no feedback for Mute/Unmute use case)
- listens for 7 seconds (7 seconds is the same time Alexa and Google Assistant use for similar features)
- any command can be used, no context knowledge of the previous use case 
- If dialog got cancelt (via PTT, Touch or by command ""Cancel"") no snoozing follows
- If dialog got cancelled due to critical restriction being active no snoozing follows
- Snoozing state can be canceled via PTT or command ""Cancel""
- During Snoozing a specific ""Snoozing"" Visual is shown. There are two different visuals available, depending on the presence of an app
- During Snoozing there is no audio ducking (attenuation of the entertainment playback)
- "Klong" sound is not used anymore
- Customer can deactivate Snoozing in the Personal Assistant Settings
- ""Snoozing Hints"" are planned to be shown with the visual so that this feature/state is easier to understand for customer
- Only the zone that activated the personal assistant before can continue with snoozing (might change in the future)

Title (EN): Provide Public Key Infrastructure
Title (DE): �ffentliche Schl�ssel-Infrastruktur bereitstellen
Description (EN): The Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) is the backend system responsible for issuing the ECU certificates needed for secure onboard communication (SecOC, IPsec, MACsec) and offboard communication (ConnectedDrive, RSU, Service29). It consists of the Certification Authority (CA) systems, which are issuing certificates, databases (Vehicle Certificate Storage Manager - VCSM), and multiple processes needed for authentication and authorization. At BMW the system running the CA for the vehicle PKI is called a Certificate-Binding-Box (CBB). BMW uses the X.509 PKI standard for certificate formats and best practices.

The BMW Vehicle PKI is structured in four hierarchy levels:
  1) The Root CA: This is the trust-anchor for the vehicle ECU certificates
  2) one CA per function, e.g., ID-CA, TLS-CA, IPsec-internal-CA
  3.1) for each BMW production plant: two SubCAs for each function
  3.2) two SubCAs for prototypes, i.e., BMW FIZ (BBG, development, TSP, etc.)
  3.3) two SubCAs for dealerships
  4) the ECU certificates, e.g., ID, TLS, IPsec-internal, etc.

After issuing the certificates inside the BMW plant or dealership, the ECU can use its certificate to authenticate against other ECUs (internal vehicle communication) or backend (ConnectedDrive). Additionally, the public/private keypair of the ECU is used by the backend (CBB) to encrypt the symmetric keys (needed for SecOC & MACsec communication) for the ECU, so the keys are protected at transfer from the backend to the ECU.
Also, the ECU certificates contain the VIN of the vehicle in which the ECU is built into, so the certificates represent a binding of an ECU (by its ECU-UID) to a vehicle (by its VIN). This VIN is for example used for the verification of Secure Token issued for a VIN (instead of an ECU-UID) or the Coding data (NCD).

Die ECU-Zertifikate enthalten auch die Fahrgestellnummer (VIN) des Fahrzeugs, in das die ECU eingebaut ist, sodass die Zertifikate eine Bindung der ECU (durch ihre ECU-UID) an ein Fahrzeug (durch die VIN) darstellen. Title (EN): Provide Public Key Infrastructure
Title (DE): �ffentliche Schl�ssel-Infrastruktur bereitstellen
Description (EN): The Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) is the backend system responsible for issuing the ECU certificates needed for secure onboard communication (SecOC, IPsec, MACsec) and offboard communication (ConnectedDrive, RSU, Service29). It consists of the Certification Authority (CA) systems, which are issuing certificates, databases (Vehicle Certificate Storage Manager - VCSM), and multiple processes needed for authentication and authorization. At BMW the system running the CA for the vehicle PKI is called a Certificate-Binding-Box (CBB). BMW uses the X.509 PKI standard for certificate formats and best practices.

The BMW Vehicle PKI is structured in four hierarchy levels:
  1) The Root CA: This is the trust-anchor for the vehicle ECU certificates
  2) one CA per function, e.g., ID-CA, TLS-CA, IPsec-internal-CA
  3.1) for each BMW production plant: two SubCAs for each function
  3.2) two SubCAs for prototypes, i.e., BMW FIZ (BBG, development, TSP, etc.)
  3.3) two SubCAs for dealerships
  4) the ECU certificates, e.g., ID, TLS, IPsec-internal, etc.

After issuing the certificates inside the BMW plant or dealership, the ECU can use its certificate to authenticate against other ECUs (internal vehicle communication) or backend (ConnectedDrive). Additionally, the public/private keypair of the ECU is used by the backend (CBB) to encrypt the symmetric keys (needed for SecOC & MACsec communication) for the ECU, so the keys are protected at transfer from the backend to the ECU.
Also, the ECU certificates contain the VIN of the vehicle in which the ECU is built into, so the certificates represent a binding of an ECU (by its ECU-UID) to a vehicle (by its VIN). This VIN is for example used for the verification of Secure Token issued for a VIN (instead of an ECU-UID) or the Coding data (NCD).

Die ECU-Zertifikate enthalten auch die Fahrgestellnummer (VIN) des Fahrzeugs, in das die ECU eingebaut ist, sodass die Zertifikate eine Bindung der ECU (durch ihre ECU-UID) an ein Fahrzeug (durch die VIN) darstellen.
